newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin doctors upbeat on surgery prospects.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin doctors upbeat on surgery prospects.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin needs time for his heart to recover from a bout of blood supply problems before a bypass operation to relieve his clogged arteries. Doctors also need to look into an unexplained blood problem.

But the Russian president's medical team, confirming their decision to operate in six to eight weeks, gave an optimistic assessment of his health on Wednesday. His liver, kidneys and brain were working normally, they said.

Michael DeBakey, the Houston-based pioneer of heart bypass surgery who has been asked by U.S. President Bill Clinton to make Yeltsin his "first priority", said he was encouraged by an improvement in the heart action but wanted an explanation for possible intestinal bleeding before operating.

"The timing for the operation is dependent to a great extent on what the medical team observes over the next six weeks in terms of correcting some of the problems that exist and in terms of preparing him for the operation," he told a news conference.
Other specialists said the delay was curious.
Hans Borst, a leading German cardiologist attending a conference in Moscow, said it was highly unusual for patients to wait more than a week, given the risk of new heart attacks.
But DeBakey said: "It's important to understand what may seem to be a delay in the operation not in terms of a delay but preparation for the operation."
Renat Akchurin, the Russian surgeon who will operate, told the news conference the wait would raise the chances of success to close to 100 percent from 80 percent at the moment.

"The encouraging aspect is the fact that his cardiac function, muscle function, has improved during the past month," DeBakey said. "That's a very good sign indicating that there is continuous improvement to take place and secondly that the operation will be even more successful."
Bypass surgery grafts veins, usually from the leg, to route blood around clogged arteries and into the heart. Yeltsin had two heart attacks last year as a result of poor blood supply.
Akchurin said at the weekend that Yeltsin probably had a third attack in late June or early July, when he suddenly dropped out of sight near the end of his reelection campaign.
DeBakey said there was evidence of a "decrease in the function of the cardiac muscle", which is usually due to weak blood flow.

But he said: "The encouraging thing about this is the fact that in the envelope between about a month ago when he may have had the damage to his myocardium (heart muscle) there has been a significant improvement in muscular function."

"This gives us good justification for prolonging this period of rehabilitation programme...to improve his condition and get him in better shape for the operation. So this is one of the basic reasons we're doing it as well as in a sense to correct these other little problems."

These were not specific heart problems and included a loss of haemoglobin, the red blood pigment that carries oxygen round the body, perhaps by intestinal bleeding. Contradicting recent rumours, DeBakey said Yeltsin had no liver or kidney trouble.
"He has kidney function, his liver functions are perfectly normal," he said. Blood vessels away from the heart were also in good condition, raising the chance of restoring circulation.

"But there was during the past month a loss of haemoglobin haematically (in blood) and we don't know exactly what caused that. The most likely thing is loss through the gastro-intestinal tract," he said.
This was not uncommon and was being treated by blood transfusions, he said.
